confidence_note: Verified against the full text on archive.org (chapter 2, The Law of the Few). The Revere and Dawes account is Gladwell's, drawn from historian David Hackett Fischer's Paul Revere's Ride; Gladwell's reading (Revere was a Connector and Maven, Dawes an ordinary man) is his interpretation. The reference TR text's 'these people are not chosen, they have recognizable traits' was not found and is dropped; Salesmen are described by Gladwell as people with the skill to persuade the unconvinced.
facts: On the same night two men rode out with the identical message, that the British were coming: Paul Revere north and west of Boston, William Dawes, a tanner, through the towns to the west.

Dawes covered just as many towns and miles, but his ride did not set the countryside afire: the local militia leaders were not alerted, and so few men from Waltham fought the next day that some historians concluded the town was pro-British; it was not, it simply was not told until too late.
Gladwell's explanation: success in a word-of-mouth epidemic depends on a few people with rare social gifts, the Law of the Few: Connectors, Mavens and Salesmen.

Revere was gregarious and intensely social: a fisherman and hunter, card player and theatre-lover, pub-goer, businessman, member of the Masonic lodge and several social clubs; historian Fischer credits him with an uncanny genius for being at the centre of events. In each town he knew whom to wake: the militia leader and the key people, whom he had mostly met and who respected him.

Of Dawes, Fischer writes that the town fathers and militia commanders in Roxbury, Brookline, Watertown and Waltham were not awakened; Gladwell thinks Dawes probably had a normal social circle and, like most people, once he left his hometown would not have known whose door to knock on.

Revere was also a Maven: in autumn 1774 he set up a secret group that met at the Green Dragon Tavern to monitor British troop movements. Maven comes from Yiddish and means one who accumulates knowledge; Mavens want to share what they know.
Gladwell summarizes: Mavens are data banks, Connectors are social glue, and Salesmen have the skill to persuade people who are unconvinced of what they hear.
scene_details: Two riders, one message, different towns
Waltham, where men did not know until too late
A secret group at the Green Dragon Tavern
A list of whose door to knock on
tension: The same urgent news, the same distance, and only one ride set off the alarm.
opening_idea: Start with Dawes, the second rider who has no monument: the same message, just as many towns.

lessons.idea: How far a message goes depends on who carries it; check whether your carrier knows whom to tell in each place.
lessons.anchor: Revere knew whom to wake in each town and Dawes, a normal man out of his hometown, did not.
lessons.everyday_example_idea: A volunteer who wants to promote a charity run sends the details to the one person who runs the neighbourhood group chats rather than posting in ten places.

reflect_final: If you had one announcement to get across to a group this month, whom would you tell first, and what makes that person someone others listen to?

use_cases.situation: Planning how to announce a change at work.
use_cases.move: Revere knew whose door to knock on in every town. List the two or three people others ask first about news here and brief them first.

use_cases.situation: You want your friends to try a new restaurant.
use_cases.move: Tell the friend who already keeps everyone's plans; ask them what they think.
Ask who in the street everyone trusts and talk to that person before putting up posters.

pocket_idea: Dawes and Revere carried the same news; Revere knew whose door to knock on. Before you announce, name your three doors.

conversation_variants.punchline_idea: Two riders carried the same news on the same night, and only the one who knew whose door to knock on is remembered.
conversation_variants.thirty_sec_idea: On the night of the British march, Paul Revere and William Dawes both rode out with the same message. Revere woke militia leaders town after town. Dawes's ride barely registered; Waltham heard too late. Gladwell says Revere was a Connector and a Maven: he knew many people and gathered information. Dawes was an ordinary man.
